title: Nextflow — Professional Tutorial for Bioinformatics & Cloud
text:
1. Introduction
Nextflow is a workflow management system for running computational pipelines. It connects analysis steps, runs them in parallel, and scales from a laptop to the cloud.

Why Nextflow exists
Bioinformatics and data pipelines often involve many steps, large datasets, and many samples. Shell scripts become hard to maintain, restart, and scale. Nextflow was built to solve reproducible, portable, parallel workflow execution.


The problem Nextflow solves








Problem
Without Nextflow
With Nextflow




Parallelism
Manual job arrays
Automatic parallel tasks


Failures
Restart from scratch
Resume from last successful step


Portability
Scripts tied to one cluster
Profiles for local, AWS, GCP


Reproducibility
Ad-hoc environments
Docker/Singularity/Conda per step


Complexity
Spaghetti bash scripts
Structured processes and channels





Where Nextflow is used in industry

Academic genomics cores — RNA-seq, WGS, single-cell pipelines
Pharma bioinformatics — target discovery, biomarker pipelines
CROs & sequencing vendors — standardized nf-core pipelines
Public health — pathogen surveillance (e.g., EPI2ME, viral pipelines)
Cloud-native labs — AWS Batch, Google Life Sciences, Kubernetes

text:
6. Basic Concepts

Process







Definition
A single computational step with inputs, outputs, and a script


Analogy
One station on a factory assembly line


Industry example
FastQC on each FASTQ file in parallel


Best practice
One logical task per process; pin container versions





Channel







Definition
An asynchronous queue connecting processes with data


Analogy
A conveyor belt carrying work items


Industry example
One channel item per patient sample


Best practice
Use tuple channels for paired-end reads





Workflow







Definition
The DAG (graph) linking processes


Analogy
The master floor plan of the factory


Industry example
QC → align → call variants → annotate


Best practice
Keep main.nf readable; modularize with include





Executor







Definition
Backend that runs tasks (local, slurm, awsbatch, etc.)


Analogy
The HR department assigning workers to stations


Industry example
awsbatch for cloud scale


Best practice
Use profiles in nextflow.config





Profile







Definition
Named configuration bundle (executor, containers, paths)


Analogy
A preset mode: “laptop” vs “cloud”


Industry example
-profile docker,aws


Best practice
Never hardcode credentials in profiles





Container directive



Definition
Docker/Singularity image used by a process


Analogy
The standardized toolbox for that station


Industry example
biocontainers/fastqc:v0.11.9_cv8


Best practice
Always specify full image tags





work/ directory



Definition
Cached task directories for resume and debugging


Analogy
The workshop floor where in-progress jobs live


Industry example
Inspected when a variant-calling step fails


Best practice
Use shared workDir on cloud; enable -resume

title: Nextflow — Professional Tutorial for Bioinformatics & Cloud
text:
7. Hands-on Examples

Example 1 — Hello World
Problem: Verify Nextflow runs locally.
Solution: Create main.nf:
#!/usr/bin/env nextflow

process sayHello {
  output:
    path 'hello.txt'

  script:
  """
  echo "Hello from Nextflow" > hello.txt
  """
}

workflow {
  sayHello()
}
Run:
nextflow run main.nf
cat work/*/hello.txt
Expected output: Hello from Nextflow



Example 2 — Parallel sample processing
Problem: Process multiple samples in parallel.
Solution:
params.samples = ['S1', 'S2', 'S3']

process greetSample {
  input:
    val sample

  output:
    stdout

  script:
  """
  echo "Processing sample ${sample}"
  """
}

workflow {
  Channel.fromList(params.samples) | greetSample | view
}
Expected result: Three lines, order may vary (parallel execution).



Example 3 — Dockerized FastQC
Problem: Run FastQC in a reproducible container.
Solution:
process runFastqc {
  container 'biocontainers/fastqc:v0.11.9_cv8'

  input:
    path fastq

  output:
    path "*.html"

  script:
  """
  fastqc ${fastq}
  """
}

workflow {
  Channel.fromPath('*.fastq.gz') | runFastqc
}
Expected result: HTML QC reports per FASTQ file.



Example 4 — Python in Nextflow
Problem: Run a Python script inside a pipeline.
Solution:
process runPython {
  container 'python:3.11-slim'

  input:
    path csv

  output:
    path 'out.txt'

  script:
  """
  python -c "import pandas as pd; df=pd.read_csv('${csv}'); print(df.shape)" > out.txt
  """
}



Example 5 — R analysis step
Problem: Execute analysis.R with Dockerized R.
Solution:
process runR {
  container 'rocker/r-ver:4.3'

  input:
    path input_csv

  output:
    path 'output.csv'

  script:
  """
  Rscript analysis.R ${input_csv} output.csv
  """
}
analysis.R:
args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
dat <- read.csv(args[1])
write.csv(summary(dat), args[2])

11. Best Practices

DO

Use -resume during development
Pin container tags on every process
Store configs in nextflow.config with profiles
Test on small datasets first
Publish reports: -with-report, -with-trace, -with-timeline
Use nf-core pipelines when applicable
Keep secrets in environment variables or secret managers



DON’T

Hardcode cloud credentials in Git
Run production on :latest containers
Ignore failed tasks in work/ without logs
Mix dev and prod buckets/workDirs
Process PHI without access controls on cloud storage



Performance tips

Maximize parallelism with channels
Use appropriate cloud instance types per process
Store references genomes on shared fast storage



Security tips

Private buckets, VPC endpoints, IAM least privilege
Encrypt data at rest and in transit
Audit Tower/Nextflow run metadata



Optimization tips

Cache aggressively with -resume
Use errorStrategy and maxRetries wisely
Profile with -with-trace before scaling

text:
14. Interview Questions

Beginner
Q1: What is Nextflow?
A: A workflow manager for parallel, reproducible data and bioinformatics pipelines.
Q2: What is a process?
A: A pipeline step with defined inputs, outputs, and execution script.
Q3: Why use containers with Nextflow?
A: To pin software versions and ensure reproducibility across environments.


Intermediate
Q4: What does -resume do?
A: Reuses cached successful tasks from previous runs, rerunning only failed or changed steps.
Q5: Explain channels.
A: Queues that pass data between processes asynchronously.
Q6: How do profiles work?
A: Named configuration sets selected via -profile for different executors and settings.


Advanced
Q7: Compare Nextflow with Snakemake.
A: Both orchestrate workflows; Nextflow emphasizes dataflow channels and cloud-native executors; Snakemake uses rule graphs — choice depends on team and ecosystem.
Q8: How would you run Nextflow on AWS Batch?
A: Configure process.executor = 'awsbatch', S3 workDir, IAM roles, and container registry access in nextflow.config.
Q9: How do you handle secrets?
A: Environment variables, AWS Secrets Manager, Vault — never commit keys to Git.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
1. Why Git matters
Imagine a statistician edits a survival-analysis program on Monday, a reviewer changes it on Tuesday, and a client asks on Friday, “Which code produced this table?” Without version control, the answer may depend on memory, file names such as analysis_final_v7_really_final.sas, and a crowded shared drive.
Git gives the team a time-stamped history of text files. It records what changed, who changed it, when it changed, and the commit message explaining why. GitHub adds a shared home for Git repositories, code review, issue tracking, automation, and controlled collaboration.
Git does not validate an analysis by itself, and a Git repository is not automatically a complete electronic record or regulated document-management system. In a regulated environment, use it with your organization’s approved procedures, access controls, review requirements, retention rules, validation evidence, and electronic-signature expectations.

Who this guide is for

Bioinformaticians building reference-genome, RNA-seq, variant-calling, or Nextflow workflows
Statisticians and biostatisticians maintaining analysis plans, simulations, and statistical programs
Clinical and statistical programmers producing SDTM, ADaM, TLFs, and submission deliverables
SAS-to-R programmers translating validated logic while keeping old and new implementations comparable
Python and R programmers developing models, reports, APIs, and data-quality checks
Bio and pharma CRO teams coordinating work across sponsors, programming teams, reviewers, and vendors

By the end, you will be able to:

Keep secrets, participant data, generated outputs, and temporary files out of source control.
Design a repository that makes an analysis reproducible and easy to audit.

The simple mental model
Think of a repository as a lab notebook for the files that define your work:








Git idea
Plain-language meaning
Life-sciences example




Repository
Project folder plus its history
An ADaM derivation project


Working tree
Files you are editing now
The R script you changed today


Staging area
Changes selected for the next snapshot
Only the reviewed analysis files


Commit
A named, permanent snapshot
“Correct censoring rule for OS”


Branch

A new subgroup analysis

A fixed name attached to a commit
v1.0.0 or submission-2026-01









Tip



The key distinction: Git is the version-control tool on your computer. GitHub is a web service that hosts Git repositories and team workflows. You can use Git without GitHub, and GitHub repositories are managed locally with Git.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
4. Install and configure Git
Check whether Git is installed:
git --version
Install Git from git-scm.com, or use your organization’s approved software process. On macOS, Xcode Command Line Tools may provide Git. On Windows, Git for Windows provides Git Bash. On Linux, use your distribution’s package manager.
Configure the identity written into your commits:
git config --global user.name "Your Full Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global pull.rebase false
Inspect the configuration:
git config --global --list
git config user.name
git config user.email
Use the email address required by your organization. A commit identity is not the same thing as authentication. GitHub authentication normally uses a browser login, SSH key, or a personal access token through an approved enterprise process. Never paste a password, token, private key, participant data, or sponsor data into a commit.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
5. Start a project safely

Option A: Start a new local project
mkdir trial-analysis
cd trial-analysis
git init
git status
git init creates the hidden .git directory that stores history. It does not upload anything and it does not create a backup by itself.
Create a small project structure:
trial-analysis/
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── data/
│   └── README.md
├── R/
├── sas/
├── python/
├── tests/
├── reports/
└── renv.lock or requirements.txt


Option B: Copy an existing GitHub project
git clone https://github.com/organization/project.git
cd project
git remote -v
Cloning downloads the project and its history. It does not give you permission to push. For a private sponsor repository, follow the approved access and authentication process.


A useful README
A good README answers: What is this project? What data may be used? How is the environment installed? How is the analysis run? What is the review status? Who owns it? What is intentionally not stored here?
# Trial analysis

Purpose: derive analysis datasets and produce descriptive tables.

## Run

1. Install the approved R/Python environment.
2. Place authorized input data in `data/` as described in `data/README.md`.
3. Run `make all` or the documented workflow command.

## Data policy

Participant-level data is not stored in this repository. Use the approved secure data location.

## Status

Code is under development. Release tags identify reviewed versions.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
6. The everyday Git workflow
The basic loop is: inspect, select, save a meaningful snapshot, share, review.
git status
git diff
git add R/derive_adam.R tests/test-derive.R
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Correct treatment-emergent event derivation"
git log --oneline --decorate --graph -10
git push origin your-branch-name

What each step protects you from

git status shows files changed, untracked, or staged.
git diff shows unstaged edits before you record them.
git add selects exactly what belongs in the next commit.
git diff --staged is the final inspection before recording the snapshot.
git commit creates a local, named checkpoint.
git log lets you see the story of the project.
git push sends local commits to the shared GitHub copy.

Write commit messages for a reviewer who was not sitting beside you:
Good: Fix missing baseline flag in ADaM derivation
Weak: changes
One commit should usually represent one coherent idea. Do not mix a censoring-rule change, a new logo, and a mass formatting rewrite in one commit.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
7. A first hands-on exercise
This exercise uses harmless text files. In a real study, use only authorized data and repositories.
mkdir git-practice
cd git-practice
git init
printf "subject_id,visit,score\n001,Baseline,10\n" > analysis-data.csv
printf "# Analysis practice\n" > README.md
git status
git add README.md analysis-data.csv
git commit -m "Add initial analysis inputs and README"
Now change the score, inspect the difference, and commit the correction:
printf "subject_id,visit,score\n001,Baseline,12\n" > analysis-data.csv
git diff
git add analysis-data.csv
git commit -m "Correct baseline score in practice data"
git log --oneline
The important lesson is not the CSV. It is the habit: make a small change, inspect it, explain it, and preserve it.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
8. Branches and pull requests
The main branch should represent the team’s trusted line of work. Create a branch for a change:
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c fix-baseline-derivation
Work, test, and commit on the branch:
git status
git add R/derive_adam.R tests/test-derive.R
git commit -m "Fix baseline derivation and add test"
git push --set-upstream origin fix-baseline-derivation
Open a pull request on GitHub. A useful pull request description states:

What changed: corrected the baseline flag for the specified visit window.
Why: the prior logic excluded valid baseline records.
Evidence: unit tests pass; comparison output is attached in the approved location.
Impact: affected dataset, tables, listings, figures, and known limitations.
Reviewers: the programmer and statistician responsible for the analysis.

Reviewers should inspect the diff, run the documented checks, consider edge cases, and record their decision. After approval and passing checks, merge according to team policy. Delete the branch only after it is no longer needed.

Feature
Practical use

For regulated teams, configure repository visibility, least-privilege access, two-factor authentication, branch protection, required reviews, status checks, & audit logging according to organizational policy. GitHub settings do not replace a validated process; they help enforce one.

text:
10. Connecting Git to reproducibility
Git can record the code, but reproducibility also depends on inputs, software versions, parameters, and execution instructions.





flowchart TD
    A[Reviewed commit] --> B[Dependency lockfile]
    A --> C[Input data version or controlled reference]
    A --> D[Parameters and analysis plan]
    B --> E[Reproducible environment]
    C --> F[Traceable inputs]
    D --> G[Traceable decisions]
    E --> H[Re-run and compare outputs]
    F --> H
    G --> H






Record the things that define an execution:

Git commit ID or release tag
R package lockfile such as renv.lock
Python dependencies such as requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, or a lockfile
SAS version and approved macros or configuration
Docker image digest where containers are used
Nextflow version, pipeline revision, parameters, and reference files
Input-data location and controlled data version, never an unauthorized copy of the data
Output checksums where appropriate

Example provenance note:
Analysis release: v1.2.0
Git commit: 8f31c2a
R: 4.4.1
Packages: renv.lock
Input snapshot: secure-data-release-2026-01
Workflow: nextflow run main.nf -r v1.2.0
Review: approved pull request #42

section: 11. Git for R, SAS, Python, and Quarto
text:
11. Git for R, SAS, Python, and Quarto

R and Quarto
Track .R, .Rmd, .qmd, project configuration, tests, and lockfiles. Do not track rendered HTML, caches, local history, or large confidential data unless the project specifically requires it.
git add analysis.qmd R/ tests/ renv.lock
git commit -m "Add reviewed descriptive statistics report"
quarto render analysis.qmd


SAS
Track .sas programs, approved macro source, metadata, test fixtures, and documentation. Coordinate line-ending and encoding conventions with the team. Keep controlled source separate from generated logs and output unless the process requires those artifacts to be retained.
git diff -- sas/adam_adsl.sas
git add sas/adam_adsl.sas
git commit -m "Derive age group using approved specification"


Python
Track .py, tests, configuration, packaging files, and dependency lockfiles. Never commit .env files containing credentials.
python -m pytest
git add src/ tests/ pyproject.toml
git commit -m "Add validation for missing laboratory values"


SAS-to-R translation
Use a branch for the translation, preserve the original specification, and create paired tests. Compare row counts, keys, variable types, missing-value behavior, sort order, and numeric results within an agreed tolerance. A successful translation is demonstrated by evidence, not by similar-looking code.

12. .gitignore: keep the repository clean
.gitignore tells Git which files should normally remain untracked. It is a convenience, not a data-security boundary.
# Operating-system and editor files
.DS_Store

# Python
__pycache__/
.venv/

# R

renv/library/

text:
13. Essential inspection commands
# Where am I and what changed?
pwd
git status --short
git diff --stat
git diff

# What has been recorded?
git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all
git show --stat HEAD
git show HEAD~1:path/to/file.R

# Which commit changed a line or file?
git log --follow -- path/to/file.R
git blame -L 20,40 path/to/file.R

# What is shared and which branch is active?
git branch --show-current
git branch -vv
git remote -v
git fetch --prune origin
git blame is a tracing tool, not a way to assign blame to a person. Use it to find the commit and discussion that explain a line.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
14. Undoing mistakes without panic
Read git status first. The right command depends on whether the change is unstaged, staged, committed locally, or already shared.
# Unstage a file, keeping its edits
git restore --staged path/to/file.R

# Discard an unstaged edit; this cannot be easily recovered
git restore path/to/file.R

# Edit the most recent commit message
git commit --amend -m "Better explanation of the change"

# Create a new commit that reverses a shared commit
git revert <commit-id>
Avoid rewriting shared history with git reset --hard or force-pushing unless your team explicitly authorizes it. For a public or regulated branch, git revert is usually easier to understand and audit.
Recover an earlier file version for inspection without changing the branch:
git show <commit-id>:path/to/file.R

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
15. Pulling, merging, and resolving conflicts
Before starting work, update your branch:
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git switch your-branch-name
git merge main
A conflict means Git found two edits to the same part of a file and cannot safely choose. Open the file and look for markers:
CURRENT_BRANCH_VERSION
======================
INCOMING_BRANCH_VERSION
Choose the correct content, remove all markers, run the relevant tests, then finish:
git add path/to/resolved-file.R
git commit
For an approved analysis, do not resolve a conflict by guessing. Ask the responsible statistician or programmer when the conflict changes derivation logic, endpoint definitions, population flags, or output meaning.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
16. Tags, releases, and traceable delivery
A tag gives a stable name to an exact commit:
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Reviewed analysis release 1.0.0"
git push origin v1.0.0
git show v1.0.0
Use a naming convention agreed by the team. For example, v1.0.0 can mean a first reviewed release, while submission-2026-01 can identify a delivery milestone. Never move a release tag silently. If a correction is needed, create a new tag and document the reason.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
section: 17. Team workflow for a CRO or pharma project
text:
17. Team workflow for a CRO or pharma project

The sponsor-approved specification and repository ownership are documented.
Access is granted to named users with the least privilege needed.
The team agrees on branches, review roles, commit messages, checks, and release tags.
A programmer creates a focused branch and links it to an issue or requirement.
The programmer commits code and tests in small, understandable units.
A reviewer checks the diff and runs documented validation steps.
The statistician or designated approver reviews the analysis impact.
The pull request is merged only after required checks and approvals pass.
A release tag, environment record, and output evidence are created.
The repository, logs, approvals, and linked artifacts are retained under the approved process.

This workflow makes a handoff easier: a new programmer can see the current state, understand why a decision was made, and reproduce the intended run without relying on an informal conversation.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
18. Common mistakes and troubleshooting

“Permission denied” when pushing
Check the remote URL and your account access:
git remote -v
git branch -vv
You may be authenticated as the wrong account, missing repository permission, or using an unapproved authentication method. Ask the repository administrator rather than sharing credentials.


“Your branch is behind”
Save your work in a commit or stash, fetch the remote, then integrate the latest approved changes:
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Save work before updating branch"
git pull --rebase origin main
Use the team’s merge or rebase policy. Do not rebase a branch that other people are actively using without coordinating.


A file still appears after .gitignore
Ignore rules do not remove files already tracked:
git rm --cached path/to/file
git commit -m "Stop tracking generated file"


A large or sensitive file was committed
Stop pushing, notify the responsible security or project contact, revoke exposed credentials, and follow the approved remediation process. History rewriting may be necessary, but it must be coordinated because it changes commit IDs and other people’s clones.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
19. Practical review checklist
Before opening a pull request, confirm:

The branch starts from the intended base branch.
The diff contains only the requested change.
No participant-level data, credentials, tokens, or private keys are included.
Tests cover changed logic and important edge cases.
R, SAS, Python, Quarto, Docker, or Nextflow versions are documented.
Variable labels, derivation rules, population flags, and output changes are explained.
The README or run instructions still work.
Generated files are handled according to project policy.
The commit and pull request messages explain purpose and impact.
The reviewer can reproduce the check from a clean checkout.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
section: 20. Mini project: a traceable analysis change
text:
20. Mini project: a traceable analysis change
Create a small repository containing a README, a script, a test, and a .gitignore. Make an intentionally small change, such as correcting the handling of a missing value. Then:

Open an issue describing the problem and expected behavior.
Create a branch named after the issue.
Add a test that demonstrates the intended behavior.
Change the analysis code.
Run the test and record the command and result.
Commit the test and code with separate, meaningful messages if appropriate.
Open a pull request with impact and evidence.
Ask a colleague to review the diff.
Merge after approval and tag the reviewed state.
Write a short provenance note with the tag, environment, inputs, and output location.

The finished repository should let another person answer: What changed? Why? Who reviewed it? Which code and environment produced the result?

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
21. Interview questions

What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
Git is a distributed version-control system. GitHub hosts repositories and provides collaboration features such as pull requests, issues, permissions, and Actions.


Why use a branch?
A branch isolates work so the trusted branch remains stable while a change is developed, tested, and reviewed.


What is a commit?
A commit is a named snapshot of selected changes, with an author, timestamp, parent history, and message.


How would you protect clinical analysis code?
Use approved access controls, protected branches, required review, traceable issues and pull requests, automated checks, release tags, dependency records, controlled data references, and documented retention and validation procedures.


What would you do after committing a token?
Treat it as exposed: revoke or rotate it immediately, notify the responsible security contact, preserve incident evidence, and follow the approved history-remediation process. Deleting the file in a new commit does not make the token safe.

title: Git and GitHub — Reproducible Collaboration for Life Sciences
text:
23. Final summary
Git is a disciplined memory for your project. GitHub turns that memory into a team practice: reviewable changes, visible decisions, automated checks, and named releases. For bioinformatics and regulated programming, the real value is not knowing every command. It is being able to connect a requirement, a change, a review, an environment, an input version, and a delivered result.
Start small: initialize one safe practice repository, make one meaningful commit, create one branch, and review one pull request. The habit scales from a personal Python script to a multi-programmer clinical submission.

title: Docker — Professional Tutorial for Life Sciences
text:
1. Introduction
Docker is a platform that packages an application and everything it needs to run — code, libraries, settings — into a portable unit called a container.

Why Docker exists
Before containers, teams struggled with a familiar problem: “It works on my machine.” Different laptops, servers, and cloud environments had different software versions. Results changed. Audits failed. Pipelines broke in production.
Docker was created to make software portable, repeatable, and isolated.


The problem Docker solves








Problem
Without Docker
With Docker




Environment differences
Results vary by machine
Same image → same behavior


Complex installs
Days installing bioinformatics tools
Pull a pre-built image in minutes


Reproducibility
Hard to prove what ran
Versioned images document the environment


Isolation
Tools conflict on one server
Each container runs independently





Where Docker is used in industry

Pharmaceutical R&D — reproducible ML and cheminformatics environments
Clinical programming — fixed R/SAS/Python stacks for TLF generation
Bioinformatics — pipelines for genomics, proteomics, and multi-omics
Healthcare AI — deploying models in controlled containers
Cloud & DevOps — AWS ECS, Google Cloud Run, Kubernetes workloads







Tip



Beginner takeaway: Docker is a standardized box for software. Same box, same result — on your laptop, a lab server, or the cloud.

title: Docker — Professional Tutorial for Life Sciences
text:
2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to

Explain what Docker is and why regulated industries use it
Install Docker Desktop on Windows, macOS, or Linux
Distinguish images, containers, registries, volumes, and networks
Build a custom image using a Dockerfile
Run, stop, and remove containers from the command line
Mount data safely without baking sensitive files into images
Describe where Docker fits in bioinformatics and clinical programming workflows
Apply industry best practices for security, GxP, and reproducibility
Troubleshoot common Docker errors
Complete a mini project: a reproducible clinical summary container

title: Docker — Professional Tutorial for Life Sciences
text:
3. Why is this important?

Why should someone learn Docker?
Docker is one of the most requested skills in bioinformatics, data engineering, and DevOps job postings. It turns fragile setups into shareable, testable environments.


Why do companies use it?

Speed — onboard new analysts in hours, not weeks
Compliance — versioned images support audit trails
Scale — same container runs on one laptop or 1,000 cloud nodes
Cost — efficient resource use compared to full virtual machines



Why is it important in bioinformatics?
Genomics pipelines combine dozens of tools (FastQC, BWA, GATK, bcftools). Docker (and Biocontainers) pins exact versions so published results can be reproduced.


Why is it important in clinical programming?
Clinical trial analysis must be reproducible. Docker ensures the same R packages, SAS components, or Python libraries are used for every database lock and QC re-run.


Why is it useful in data science?
Data scientists package models with dependencies so staging and production environments match — reducing “model works locally but fails in deployment” issues.

6. Basic Concepts

Image







Definition
Read-only template containing an app and its dependencies


Analogy
A sealed recipe kit with pre-measured ingredients


Industry example
rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 for a locked clinical R environment


Best practice
Always use specific version tags — never :latest in production





Container







Definition
A running instance of an image


Analogy
The actual meal cooked from the recipe kit


Industry example
One container per study analysis run


Best practice
Use --rm for temporary jobs; name containers in long-running services





Registry







Definition
Storage and distribution system for images


Analogy
A warehouse catalog of standardized boxes


Industry example
Private AWS ECR registry for validated pharma images


Best practice
Use private registries for internal and GxP workloads





Docker Hub







Definition
Public registry maintained by Docker


Analogy
An app store for container images


Industry example
Pulling official python:3.11-slim base images


Best practice
Prefer verified publishers; scan images for vulnerabilities





Dockerfile







Definition
Text file with step-by-step instructions to build an image


Analogy
The master recipe card


Industry example
Documented build file archived with study deliverables


Best practice
Keep Dockerfiles in version control; review changes like code





Volume







Definition
Persistent storage mounted into a container


Analogy
A USB drive plugged into the box


Industry example
Mount clinical CSV input and TLF output folders


Best practice
Never store patient data inside the image — mount at runtime





Network







Definition
Virtual network allowing containers to communicate


Analogy
Phone lines between offices in the same building


Industry example
Connect a Shiny app container to a PostgreSQL container


Best practice
Use custom networks; avoid exposing unnecessary ports

7. Hands-on Examples

Example 1 — Hello World
Problem: Confirm Docker is installed and working.
Solution: Run the official test image.
docker run hello-world
Expected output: Message containing Hello from Docker!
Explanation: Docker downloaded a tiny image, started a container, printed output, and exited.



Example 2 — Run R without installing R
Problem: You need R 4.3 but do not want to install it locally.
Solution:
docker run --rm rocker/r-ver:4.3 R --version
Expected output: R version 4.3.x ...
Explanation: The container includes R; your host machine stays unchanged.



Example 3 — Interactive Python shell
Problem: Test Python in an isolated environment.
Solution:
docker run -it --rm python:3.11-slim python
print("Docker Python ready")
exit()
Expected result: Python REPL opens, prints message, exits cleanly.



Example 4 — Build a clinical summary image
Problem: Create a reproducible environment for summarizing patient ages.
Solution:
Create summarize.R:
args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
dat <- read.csv(args[1])
out <- data.frame(
  n = nrow(dat),
  mean_age = round(mean(dat$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
)
write.csv(out, args[2], row.names = FALSE)
cat("Done\n")
Create patients.csv:
patient_id,age
001,54
002,61
003,47
Create Dockerfile:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.3

A: An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance of that image.
Q2: What is Docker Hub?

Q3: Why do bioinformatics teams use Docker?
A: To pin tool versions and reproduce pipeline results across machines.


Intermediate
Q4: What is a volume and when would you use one?
A: Persistent storage mounted into a container — used for input data and output results without baking them into the image.
Q5: How do Docker and Kubernetes relate?
A: Docker builds/runs containers locally; Kubernetes orchestrates many containers across a cluster.
Q6: How would you make a clinical analysis reproducible with Docker?
A: Build a versioned image, document the tag/digest, mount study data at runtime, archive the Dockerfile in version control.


Advanced
Q7: What are multi-stage builds?
A: Dockerfiles with multiple FROM stages — compile in one stage, copy only artifacts to a smaller final image.
Q8: How do you reduce attack surface in production containers?
A: Non-root user, minimal base image, no secrets in layers, regular scanning, read-only filesystem where possible.
Q9: Explain how Nextflow uses Docker.
A: Each process specifies a container image; Nextflow pulls and runs it per task, enabling reproducible scalable pipelines.

If Python is available, Quarto can run it and include the output.

Again: **this is optional** for beginners.

---

## 14. A text-only beginner example

Create a file named `intro.qmd`:

```markdown
---
title: "Introduction to Quarto"
format: html
---

# Welcome

Quarto helps you create beautiful documents.

---

## Try R (optional)

If you want to try a few simple R examples without installing R, open the dedicated R page with short notes and an in-browser WebR playground: [R — Getting Started](r.qmd).

The playground runs small R snippets using WebR (R compiled to WebAssembly) and is intended for quick practice and learning. For larger work, consider Binder or RStudio Cloud.

## What I learned

- Quarto uses `.qmd` files
- Markdown is easy to write
- I can create HTML pages
- I do not need R to begin

## My Next Step

I will learn how to add images and tables.
```

Render it:

```bash
quarto render intro.qmd
```

---

## 15. Creating different output formats

One powerful feature of Quarto is that you can generate different types of output.

### HTML
```yaml
format: html
```

### PDF
```yaml
format: pdf
```

### Word
```yaml
format: docx
```

### Multiple formats
```yaml
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
  docx: default
```

Then run:

```bash
quarto render yourfile.qmd
```

### Important note about PDF
Creating PDFs usually requires a LaTeX installation such as TinyTeX.

If PDF rendering fails, start with HTML first.

---

## 16. Working with sections

A bigger document can be organized into sections.

Example:

```markdown
# Chapter 1
## Topic 1.1
## Topic 1.2

# Chapter 2
## Topic 2.1
```

This structure helps readers navigate your content.

In HTML output, Quarto may also generate a table of contents.

---

## 17. Adding a table of contents

You can enable it in YAML:

```yaml
---
title: "My Tutorial"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
---
```

This adds a table of contents automatically.

---

## 18. Changing theme and appearance

For HTML documents, you can choose themes.

Example:

```yaml
---
title: "Styled Document"
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
---
```

Some common themes:
- cosmo
- litera
- flatly
- darkly
- minty

You can experiment and see which one you like.

---

## 19. Creating a presentation

Quarto can create slides too.

Example:

```markdown
---
title: "My First Presentation"
format: revealjs
---

# Slide 1
Welcome to my presentation.

# Slide 2
- Point one
- Point two
```

Render it and Quarto will create a slide deck.

---

## 20. Creating a website

Quarto can also build websites.

A basic website project often includes:
- `_quarto.yml`
- `index.qmd`
- other `.qmd` pages

Example `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "My Website"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    toc: true
```

Example `index.qmd`:

```markdown
---
title: "Home"
---

# Welcome

This is my Quarto website.
```

This is more advanced, but it shows how powerful Quarto is.

---

## 21. What is `_quarto.yml`?

When you work on a Quarto project with multiple files, `_quarto.yml` is the main configuration file.

It can define:
- project type
- website settings
- book settings
- output format defaults
- themes
- navigation

Think of it as the project control file.

---

## 22. How Quarto is different from Word

In Word, you usually format things visually.

In Quarto, you write simple plain text with lightweight formatting.

### Benefits of Quarto
- easier version control with Git and GitHub
- reusable documents
- cleaner structure
- can combine writing and code
- easier to publish online

At first it may feel unfamiliar, but many people find it easier over time.

---

## 23. Beginner workflow

Here is a simple beginner workflow:

1. Install Quarto
2. Create a `.qmd` file
3. Write Markdown content
4. Add YAML at the top
5. Render the file to HTML
6. Open the output in a browser
7. Edit and render again

This is enough to get started.

---

## 24. Common beginner mistakes

### Mistake 1: Forgetting the YAML lines
YAML must start and end with `---`.

### Mistake 2: Wrong file extension
Use `.qmd`, not `.txt`.

### Mistake 3: PDF not rendering
This often happens because LaTeX is not installed.

### Mistake 4: Broken image path
Make sure the image file path is correct.

### Mistake 5: Expecting code to run without installing Python or R
If you want executable code blocks, you need the related language installed.

---

## 25. Example: A small personal profile page

Create `profile.qmd`:

```markdown
---
title: "My Profile"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
---

# About Me

My name is Praveen.

I am learning Quarto to create documents and websites.

## Skills I Want to Learn

- Quarto
- Markdown
- GitHub
- Python

## Favorite Resources

- [Quarto](https://quarto.org)
- [Markdown Guide](https://www.markdownguide.org)
```

Render it:

```bash
quarto render profile.qmd
```

---

## 26. Example: A study notes document

```markdown
---
title: "Study Notes"
format: html
---

# Chapter 1

This chapter explains the basics.

## Key Points

- Point A
- Point B
- Point C

## Summary

This chapter introduced the main ideas.
```

This is useful for students and self-learners.

---

## 27. If you later want to learn code in Quarto

Once you are comfortable with text and Markdown, you can gradually add code.

### Python example

````markdown
```python
name = "Praveen"
print("Hello", name)
```



```r
x <- 10
x + 5
```
But remember: learning Quarto does not require learning R first.

text:
Welcome! This is not just code snippets. You’ll learn R the way professionals do: by understanding why we use each concept, with real-world stories, before writing a single line of code.
Whether you’re a clinical programmer, SAS expert, statistician, or complete beginner—this tutorial is designed for you.





Imagine you’re a clinical researcher with patient data from 5,000 subjects. You need to: - Clean messy data (missing values, typos, wrong formats) - Calculate statistics (mean, median, confidence intervals) - Create visualizations (plots, charts, tables) - Generate a report with all results
In SAS: You’d write 50+ lines of PROC code, manage libraries, and wait for compilation.
In R: You load a dataset, clean it, analyze it, and visualize it—all in 20 lines. The results appear instantly.
R is a language designed by statisticians FOR statisticians. It’s like having a super-smart assistant who: - Understands data intuitively - Can do complex math instantly - Creates beautiful visualizations - Scales from small datasets to millions of rows - Works on any device (Windows, Mac, Linux)

# Now calculate dose per kg
dose_per_kg <- drug_dose / patient_weight
print(dose_per_kg)  # Output: 2.94 mg/kg
Why this matters: If the dose changes from 250 to 300, you only change ONE number. The calculation updates automatically.

hemoglobin <- 8.5

This is how clinical algorithms work: compare, calculate, decide.

When to use: Measurements, calculations, weights, heights, lab values, temperatures

R has a helper function to tell you:

class(1001)           # "numeric" (even though it's a whole number!)

class("Alice")        # "character"
class(TRUE)           # "logical"







A vector is like a shopping list: - All items are groceries (same type) - Each item is separate but in the same list - You can count them, sort them, or find specific ones
Think of patient data from a clinical trial:
# Cholesterol levels for 5 patients
cholesterol <- c(210, 195, 240, 185, 220)
That’s a vector of 5 numbers.

# NEW WAY (using a vector):
glucose_readings <- c(245, 238, 225, 212, 198, 185)
avg <- mean(glucose_readings)  # Automatic!
print(avg)  # 217.17





cholesterol <- c(210, 195, 240, 185, 220, 205)

mean(cholesterol)      # Average: 209.17 (normal for many)
median(cholesterol)    # Middle value: 212.5

min(cholesterol)       # Lowest: 185
max(cholesterol)       # Highest: 240

cholesterol[1]        # First patient: 210
cholesterol[3]        # Third patient: 240
cholesterol[c(1,3)]   # First AND third: 210, 240
cholesterol[-2]       # Everyone EXCEPT second: 210, 240, 185, 220, 205



high_cholesterol <- cholesterol > 200
print(high_cholesterol)  # TRUE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE

# Get the actual values
cholesterol[cholesterol > 200]  # 210, 240, 220, 205




# Blood pressure readings for 8 patients
systolic <- c(120, 145, 138, 148, 110, 155, 142, 130)

# Who has stage 2 hypertension (>140)?
high_bp <- systolic > 140
print(high_bp)  # FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE

# How many patients are at risk?
num_at_risk <- sum(high_bp)  # Counts TRUE values
print(num_at_risk)  # 3 patients need intervention

# What are their exact readings?
risky_readings <- systolic[systolic > 140]
print(risky_readings)  # 145, 148, 155, 142
This is how clinical alerts work—R automatically finds the patients who need attention!







A data frame is like an Excel spreadsheet: - Rows = individual records (patients, visits, observations) - Columns = variables (name, age, diagnosis, treatment) - Different columns can have different types (numbers, text, dates)



You’re conducting a diabetes study tracking:
# Create a dataset of 4 patients
patients <- data.frame(
  patient_id = c(1001, 1002, 1003, 1004),
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana"),
  age = c(52, 45, 58, 50),
  glucose_baseline = c(245, 198, 310, 225),
  treatment = c("Drug_A", "Drug_B", "Drug_A", "Placebo"),
  improved = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

# View the full dataset
print(patients)
Output:

1        1001   Alice  52              245    Drug_A     TRUE
2        1002     Bob  45              198    Drug_B    FALSE
3        1003 Charlie  58              310    Drug_A     TRUE
4        1004   Diana  50              225   Placebo    FALSE



# Get one column
patients$name              # "Alice" "Bob" "Charlie" "Diana"

# Get specific rows
patients[1, ]              # First patient's entire row
patients[c(1,3), ]         # First AND third patient

# Get specific cell
patients[2, 3]             # Bob's age: 45

# Logical indexing (find all improved patients)
improved_patients <- patients[patients$improved == TRUE, ]

# Calculate average baseline glucose
avg_glucose <- mean(patients$glucose_baseline)
print(avg_glucose)  # 244.5 mg/dL



# A hospital has 3 patients in a medication trial
trial_data <- data.frame(
  patient = c("P001", "P002", "P003"),
  medication = c("Aspirin_100mg", "Aspirin_100mg", "Placebo"),
  baseline_heart_rate = c(72, 88, 75),
  day_7_heart_rate = c(70, 85, 76),
  adverse_events = c("None", "Headache", "None")
)

# Question: Did Aspirin patients improve?
aspirin_group <- trial_data[trial_data$medication == "Aspirin_100mg", ]

# Calculate average improvement
baseline_avg <- mean(aspirin_group$baseline_heart_rate)
day7_avg <- mean(aspirin_group$day_7_heart_rate)
improvement <- baseline_avg - day7_avg

print(paste("Aspirin patients improved by", round(improvement, 1), "bpm"))
# Output: "Aspirin patients improved by 3.5 bpm"







A function is like a recipe or vending machine: - Input: Ingredients (or coins) - Process: Follow instructions (or mechanism) - Output: Result (meal or snack)



Instead of writing the same calculation 50 times:
# OLD (repetitive, error-prone)
result1 <- (value1 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
result2 <- (value2 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
result3 <- (value3 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
# ... repeated 50 more times!
Write it ONCE as a function:
# NEW (clean, reusable)
normalize_value <- function(value, min_val, max_val) {
  result <- (value - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
  return(result)
}

# Now use it 50 times easily
result1 <- normalize_value(value1, 0, 100)
result2 <- normalize_value(value2, 0, 100)
result3 <- normalize_value(value3, 0, 100)



# BMI = weight (kg) / (height (m))^2
# Instead of calculating this for every patient...

calculate_bmi <- function(weight_kg, height_cm) {
  height_m <- height_cm / 100
  bmi <- weight_kg / (height_m ^ 2)
  return(bmi)
}

# Now use it for any patient
bmi_alice <- calculate_bmi(75, 170)     # 26.0
bmi_bob <- calculate_bmi(82, 175)       # 26.8
bmi_charlie <- calculate_bmi(95, 180)   # 29.3

print(bmi_alice)    # 26.0
print(bmi_bob)      # 26.8
print(bmi_charlie)  # 29.3



In clinical trials, you often use the same dosing formula:
# Default: Adult dosing
calculate_dose <- function(patient_weight, dose_per_kg = 5) {
  total_dose <- patient_weight * dose_per_kg
  return(total_dose)
}

# Adult (75 kg): standard dose is 375 mg
adult_dose <- calculate_dose(75)  # Uses default 5 mg/kg
print(adult_dose)  # 375

# Child (30 kg): might need different dose
child_dose <- calculate_dose(30, dose_per_kg = 3)  # Custom 3 mg/kg
print(child_dose)  # 90







Programs need to make decisions like a nurse: - IF patient temperature > 38°C, THEN alert doctor - IF glucose < 70 mg/dL, THEN give sugar tablet - IF medication available, THEN prescribe it



patient_temp <- 39.2  # Celsius

if (patient_temp > 38.5) {
  print("ALERT: Fever detected! Notify physician!")
} else if (patient_temp > 37.5) {
  print("WARNING: Slight elevation. Monitor closely.")
} else {
  print("Normal temperature.")
}

# Output: "ALERT: Fever detected! Notify physician!"



# Diabetes risk assessment
age <- 52
fasting_glucose <- 245
family_history <- TRUE

if (fasting_glucose > 200 & age > 45) {
  risk <- "High"
} else if (fasting_glucose > 150) {
  risk <- "Moderate"
} else {
  risk <- "Low"
}

print(paste("Risk level:", risk))
# Output: "Risk level: High"



# Lab test result classification
test_result <- 8.5  # Hemoglobin g/dL

if (test_result < 7) {
  severity <- "Critical"
} else if (test_result < 8) {
  severity <- "Severe"
} else if (test_result < 10) {
  severity <- "Moderate"
} else if (test_result < 12) {
  severity <- "Mild"
} else {
  severity <- "Normal"
}

# OR use switch with intervals:
get_severity <- function(hgb) {
  if (hgb < 7) return("Critical")
  if (hgb < 8) return("Severe")
  if (hgb < 10) return("Moderate")
  if (hgb < 12) return("Mild")
  return("Normal")
}

print(get_severity(8.5))  # "Moderate"







A loop is like reading a checklist: - “Check blood pressure for patient 1” - “Check blood pressure for patient 2” - …repeat for all 100 patients



You need to check 5 patients’ lab results:
# WITHOUT loop (tedious)
glucose_1 <- 245
status_1 <- if (glucose_1 > 200) "At Risk" else "Normal"

glucose_2 <- 198
status_2 <- if (glucose_2 > 200) "At Risk" else "Normal"

glucose_3 <- 310
status_3 <- if (glucose_3 > 200) "At Risk" else "Normal"
# ... repeat 47 more times for 50 patients!

# WITH loop (clean)
glucose_readings <- c(245, 198, 310, 185, 225)

for (glucose in glucose_readings) {
  if (glucose > 200) {
    print(paste("Glucose:", glucose, "→ AT RISK"))
  } else {
    print(paste("Glucose:", glucose, "→ Normal"))
  }
}

# Output:
# Glucose: 245 → AT RISK
# Glucose: 198 → Normal
# Glucose: 310 → AT RISK
# Glucose: 185 → Normal
# Glucose: 225 → AT RISK



# Check all patients in a clinical trial
trial <- data.frame(
  patient = c("P001", "P002", "P003"),
  bmi = c(24.5, 32.1, 26.8)
)

for (i in 1:nrow(trial)) {
  patient_id <- trial[i, "patient"]
  bmi_value <- trial[i, "bmi"]
  
  if (bmi_value > 30) {
    print(paste(patient_id, "is obese (BMI =", bmi_value, ")"))
  } else {
    print(paste(patient_id, "is normal (BMI =", bmi_value, ")"))
  }
}

# Output:
# P001 is normal (BMI = 24.5 )
# P002 is obese (BMI = 32.1 )
# P003 is normal (BMI = 26.8 )







Clinical data often includes notes, diagnoses, and comments. R can: - Combine text (concatenate) - Extract parts of text - Search for patterns - Replace words



first_name <- "John"
last_name <- "Smith"
diagnosis <- "Type 2 Diabetes"

# Combine text
full_note <- paste(first_name, last_name, "diagnosed with", diagnosis)
print(full_note)
# Output: "John Smith diagnosed with Type 2 Diabetes"

# Extract parts
text <- "Patient: John Smith, Age: 52, Diagnosis: HTN"
name_part <- substr(text, 9, 19)  # Extract "John Smith"
print(name_part)

# Replace text
original <- "The patient has diabtes"  # Typo
corrected <- gsub("diabtes", "diabetes", original)
print(corrected)
# Output: "The patient has diabetes"



# Lab report text
report <- "WBC: 7.5 K/uL, Hemoglobin: 14.2 g/dL, Platelets: 250 K/uL"

# Check if abnormal values are mentioned
is_normal <- !grepl("abnormal|low|high", report, ignore.case=TRUE)
print(is_normal)  # TRUE (no abnormal values flagged)

# Count number of tests
num_tests <- length(strsplit(report, ",")[[1]])
print(num_tests)  # 3 tests reported







Clinical research involves timing: - When was a patient enrolled? - How many days until follow-up? - What’s the time between baseline and week 12?

text:
A function is like a recipe or vending machine: - Input: Ingredients (or coins) - Process: Follow instructions (or mechanism) - Output: Result (meal or snack)



Instead of writing the same calculation 50 times:
# OLD (repetitive, error-prone)
result1 <- (value1 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
result2 <- (value2 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
result3 <- (value3 - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
# ... repeated 50 more times!
Write it ONCE as a function:
# NEW (clean, reusable)
normalize_value <- function(value, min_val, max_val) {
  result <- (value - min_val) / (max_val - min_val)
  return(result)
}

# Now use it 50 times easily
result1 <- normalize_value(value1, 0, 100)
result2 <- normalize_value(value2, 0, 100)
result3 <- normalize_value(value3, 0, 100)



# BMI = weight (kg) / (height (m))^2
# Instead of calculating this for every patient...

calculate_bmi <- function(weight_kg, height_cm) {
  height_m <- height_cm / 100
  bmi <- weight_kg / (height_m ^ 2)
  return(bmi)
}

# Now use it for any patient
bmi_alice <- calculate_bmi(75, 170)     # 26.0
bmi_bob <- calculate_bmi(82, 175)       # 26.8
bmi_charlie <- calculate_bmi(95, 180)   # 29.3

print(bmi_alice)    # 26.0
print(bmi_bob)      # 26.8
print(bmi_charlie)  # 29.3



In clinical trials, you often use the same dosing formula:
# Default: Adult dosing
calculate_dose <- function(patient_weight, dose_per_kg = 5) {
  total_dose <- patient_weight * dose_per_kg
  return(total_dose)
}

# Adult (75 kg): standard dose is 375 mg
adult_dose <- calculate_dose(75)  # Uses default 5 mg/kg
print(adult_dose)  # 375

# Child (30 kg): might need different dose
child_dose <- calculate_dose(30, dose_per_kg = 3)  # Custom 3 mg/kg
print(child_dose)  # 90
