title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Important



This chapter turns statistics into intuition first, formulas second. The examples are deliberately real-world and a little playful, but the definitions stay mathematically correct.

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Part 1: Foundations of Data Analysis

1. Descriptive vs. Inferential Statistics
Think of statistics as two different jobs.
Fun example first: imagine you run a cafe and record sales for 30 days.

Descriptive statistics = your monthly report card.
Inferential statistics = using those 30 days to predict next month.
Descriptive statistics summarize what you already have. It is the profile grid of your data: counts, averages, percentages, and spread.
Inferential statistics use a sample to make a claim about a larger population. It is the part where you see a few posts and try to guess the whole story.









Concept
What it does
Real-life example




Descriptive
Summarizes observed data
Average likes on your last 20 posts


Inferential
Generalizes from sample to population
Predicting how all users might behave from a test group





2. Measures of Central Tendency
Central tendency tells you where the center of the data lives.
Fun example first: five delivery times are 12, 13, 13, 14, and 45 minutes (one rider got stuck in traffic).

Mean: the arithmetic average. It is the ultimate compromise, but it is sensitive to extreme outliers.
Median: the middle value after sorting. It is much more stable when one value is wildly unusual.
Mode: the most frequent value. It is the crowd favorite.

Example: if five friends pick restaurant budgets of $20, $25, $25, $30, and $5000, the mean is dragged upward by the billionaire, while the median stays near the center.
Formula:
\[\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\]
ML/AI use: median is often safer than mean when preprocessing skewed features.


3. Measures of Dispersion
Dispersion tells you how spread out the data is.
Fun example first: two classes can both have average score 70, but one class is tightly clustered near 70 and the other ranges from 20 to 100.

Range: the distance between the largest and smallest values.
Mean deviation: average distance from the center.
Variance and standard deviation: the core measures of spread.
Quartile deviation: focuses on the middle 50% and is less affected by outliers.

For sample data, variance is usually written as:
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\]
and standard deviation is:
\[s = \sqrt{s^2}\]
Low spread means consistency. High spread means chaos, or at least a very eventful day.
ML/AI use: standardization scales features using standard deviation.


4. Skewness and Kurtosis
Shape matters as much as center and spread.
Fun example first:

App session length is usually right-skewed (many short visits, few very long users).
Daily stock returns often have heavy tails (big surprises happen more than normal models expect).
Zero skewness: symmetric data, like a well-balanced mountain.
Positive skewness: long tail to the right. Income data is the classic example because a small number of very large values stretch the tail.
Negative skewness: long tail to the left. Early retirement ages can create this shape.
Leptokurtic: sharp peak and heavy tails. Crypto returns are a memorable example.
Platykurtic: flatter shape with lighter tails. Daily temperatures in a mild climate often feel this way.

Formulas:
\[\text{Skewness} = g_1 = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^3}{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\right)^{3/2}}\]
\[\text{Excess Kurtosis} = g_2 = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^4}{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\right)^2} - 3\]
flowchart LR
    A[Skewness = Direction of Tail] --> B[Left Tail Long = Negative Skew]
    A --> C[Balanced = Near Zero Skew]
    A --> D[Right Tail Long = Positive Skew]
ML/AI use: skewed features often benefit from log or power transforms.

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Part 2: Probability, Sampling, and Testing

5. Probability
Probability quantifies uncertainty.
Fun example first: before seeing the weather app, you estimate rain chance from the sky. After seeing dark clouds plus forecast, you update your belief.

Classical probability assumes equally likely outcomes. A fair coin has a \(1/2\) chance of landing heads.
Conditional probability updates the odds after new information arrives.

If the sky is cloudy, the chance of carrying an umbrella changes. The data is the same object, but the context is different, so the probability changes too.
Core formulas:
\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\]
\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\]
ML/AI use: conditional probability powers Naive Bayes classifiers.


6. Distribution and Sampling
In the real world, you usually cannot inspect every member of the population, so you sample.
Fun example first: tasting one spoon of soup is sampling; tasting every spoon is impossible.

Population: the full group you care about.
Sample: a smaller group you actually observe.
Distribution: how values are spread across the scale.

The Central Limit Theorem says that the distribution of sample means tends toward normality as sample size grows, even if the original data is messy.
\[\bar{X} \approx N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]
That is why repeated spoonfuls of soup can reveal the flavor of the entire pot.
ML/AI use: many confidence intervals and test statistics rely on this idea.


7. Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Tests
Use the test that matches your data, not the one that looks smartest in a slide deck.
Fun example first: if shoe sizes look reasonably bell-shaped, use parametric tests; if ratings are weird and heavily skewed, rank-based tests are safer.

Parametric tests assume structure: often normality, equal variance, and other mathematical conditions. Examples include the t-test and ANOVA.
Non-parametric tests are more flexible and often rely on ranks rather than raw values. Examples include Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis.

When the data is tidy, parametric tests are powerful. When the data is messy, non-parametric tests are often safer.


8. Hypothesis Testing
Hypothesis testing asks whether an observed effect is likely real or just noise.
Fun example first: did your new landing page actually increase signups, or did you get lucky this week?

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): no effect, no change, no difference.
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)): there is an effect.
p-value: how surprising the observed result would be if \(H_0\) were true.

Important reviewer note: a p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is a probability under the assumption that the null is true.
If the p-value is small enough for your chosen threshold, you reject the null and move forward with the stronger claim.
Common test statistic:
\[z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\]
ML/AI use: A/B tests in product analytics are hypothesis tests.


9. Type I and Type II Errors
Even good tests can make mistakes.
Fun example first: spam filters.

Marking a good email as spam is a Type I error.
Missing a spam email is a Type II error.
Type I error: false positive. You reject \(H_0\) even though it is actually true.
Type II error: false negative. You fail to reject \(H_0\) even though it is false.

Smoke alarms are the perfect metaphor: one false alarm is annoying, but ignoring a real fire is much worse.
Power reminder:
\[\text{Power} = 1 - \beta\]
ML/AI use: threshold tuning is essentially balancing these errors.


10. ANOVA
If you want to compare more than two group means, ANOVA is the right tool.
Fun example first: three ad creatives, one budget, one KPI. ANOVA checks if at least one creative truly performs differently.
Instead of running many t-tests and inflating error risk, ANOVA compares:

variation between groups
variation within groups

The big question is simple: is at least one group genuinely different?
Example: if you test four diet plans at once, ANOVA tells you whether one of them stands out without turning the analysis into a pile of pairwise comparisons.
Formula:
\[F = \frac{\text{MS}_{\text{between}}}{\text{MS}_{\text{within}}}\]
ML/AI use: quick feature screening across multiple group labels.


11. Chi-Square Test
Chi-square is for categorical data.
Fun example first: are subscription tiers independent of preferred device type (mobile, desktop, tablet)?

Chi-square test of independence checks whether two categorical variables are related.
Chi-square goodness-of-fit checks whether observed category counts match an expected pattern.

Example: does relationship status depend on zodiac sign, or are the categories unrelated? Chi-square answers that with counts, not averages.
Formula:
\[\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}\]
ML/AI use: feature-label association checks for categorical variables.

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Part 3: Correlation, Regression, and Modeling

12. Correlation and Regression
Fun example first: ice cream sales and temperature rise together, but temperature is the hidden driver.

Correlation measures strength and direction of association, from \(-1\) to \(+1\).
Regression builds an equation to predict one variable from another.

Positive correlation means two variables move together. Negative correlation means one rises while the other falls. Zero correlation means there is no linear relationship.
Reviewer note: correlation is not causation. Two variables can move together because of a hidden third factor, coincidence, or shared trend.
Key formulas:
\[r = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2\sum (y_i-\bar{y})^2}}\]
\[\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
ML/AI use: correlation heatmaps help detect redundant features.


13. Correlation Types for Real Data
Fun example first: leaderboard ranks are not evenly spaced numbers, so rank correlation is often better than Pearson.

Pearson: linear relationship on numeric values.
Spearman: monotonic relationship on ranks.
Kendall: rank agreement strength, robust for small samples.

Quick rule:

Use Pearson for roughly linear, continuous features.
Use Spearman/Kendall when outliers or nonlinearity make raw values unreliable.

ML/AI use: Spearman is common in feature engineering sanity checks.


14. Regression Assumptions
Linear regression works best when its assumptions are respected.

Linearity: the relationship should be roughly straight.
Independence of errors: one residual should not predict the next.
Homoscedasticity: the error spread should stay roughly constant.
Normality of residuals: the errors should look approximately normal.

If the fit is a highway, the road should not turn into a rollercoaster with widening lanes and echoing bumps.
Residual idea:
\[e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]
ML/AI use: residual diagnostics catch model misspecification early.


15. Data Transformation for Regression
Sometimes a transform makes the pattern visible.
Fun example first: if influencer follower counts range from 200 to 20 million, raw scale hides useful patterns.

Log transform: compresses large values and reduces skew.
Square root transform: useful for moderate right-skew.
Power transform: stretches or compresses the scale to improve linearity.

Example: log-transforming income can make the difference between regular salaries and billionaire wealth easier to model.
Formula:
\[x' = \log(x + c)\]


16. Dummy Variables
Regression wants numbers, so categorical variables need encoding.
Fun example first: for color = {red, blue, green}, do not feed words directly to linear models.

Use 1 for presence of a category.
Use 0 for absence.
Drop one reference category to avoid perfect multicollinearity.

If you have VIP, VVIP, and General membership, you only need two dummy variables. The omitted category becomes the baseline.


17. Variable Selection
Not every available feature deserves a seat in the model.
Fun example first: packing for travel with one small bag forces you to keep only useful items.

Forward selection starts small and adds useful variables.
Backward elimination starts large and removes weak variables.
Stepwise selection adds and removes variables as it goes.

Think of it like packing for a trip: the goal is to bring the essentials, not the entire closet.
ML/AI use: combine statistical selection with cross-validation, not p-values alone.


18. Logistic Regression
When the outcome is binary, logistic regression is the right fit.
Fun example first: will a customer churn this month: yes or no?
It converts a linear score into a probability using the sigmoid curve:
\[p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\]
Example: should a user buy or not buy, click or not click, stay or leave? Logistic regression gives a probability, then a threshold turns that probability into a class.
Log-odds form:
\[\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \cdots + \beta_kx_k\]

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
section: Part 4: Classification, Clustering, and Time Series
text:
Part 4: Classification, Clustering, and Time Series

19. Discriminant Analysis
Discriminant analysis separates known classes using the features that best distinguish them.
The Sorting Hat metaphor works well here: you already know the possible houses, and the model helps decide where a new person belongs.


20. Cluster Analysis
Cluster analysis finds natural groupings when the data has no labels.
Fun example first: at a food festival, people naturally gather by cuisine preference.
Example: people at a music festival cluster into different crowds based on taste, dress, and behavior. The algorithm groups similar points together using distance or similarity.
K-means objective:
\[\min \sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{x_i \in C_j} ||x_i - \mu_j||^2\]
ML/AI use: customer segmentation, anomaly pre-grouping, and recommendation bootstrapping.


21. Time Series and Forecasting
Time series data has order, not just values.
Fun example first: coffee sales peak every Monday morning and dip on Sundays.

Trend: long-term direction.
Seasonality: repeating calendar pattern.
Cyclical: longer waves without fixed timing.
Noise: the random part.

Example: winter coats spike every December, but an unexpected supply shock or pandemic can create irregular movement on top of the usual pattern.
Simple additive model:
\[Y_t = T_t + S_t + C_t + E_t\]


22. Model Evaluation
Once you build a model, you need to score it properly.
Fun example first: a medical test that predicts “healthy” for everyone can still look good on raw accuracy if disease is rare.

Confusion matrix: TP, TN, FP, FN.
Accuracy: overall correctness.
Precision: how many predicted positives were actually positive.
Recall: how many actual positives were found.
F1-score: balance between precision and recall.
ROC-AUC: how well the model ranks positives above negatives across thresholds.

If a disease screening model predicts “healthy” for almost everyone, accuracy can look excellent while the model still fails the people who need help. That is why precision, recall, and AUC matter.
Formulas:
\[\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\]
\[\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\]
\[F_1 = 2\cdot\frac{\text{Precision}\cdot\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}\]
flowchart LR
    A[Predicted Positive] --> B[True Positive]
    A --> C[False Positive]
    D[Predicted Negative] --> E[True Negative]
    D --> F[False Negative]

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
section: Part 5: Fun Statistical Methods for ML and AI
text:
Part 5: Fun Statistical Methods for ML and AI

23. Bayes Theorem and Naive Bayes
Fun example first: a movie recommender updates your “will like sci-fi” probability after seeing you watched three space movies this week.
Bayes theorem:
\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}\]
Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class.
ML/AI use: text classification, spam detection, baseline classifiers.


24. Confidence Intervals
Fun example first: your app conversion is 8%, but the interval says true performance likely sits between 7.2% and 8.8%.
95% CI for a mean (large sample):
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{0.975}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
ML/AI use: report uncertainty, not just point estimates.


25. Bootstrapping
Fun example first: you repeatedly refill a sample bag from itself to see how stable your metric is.
Process:

Sample with replacement from data.
Compute metric each time.
Use the distribution of metrics for intervals.

ML/AI use: robust uncertainty when analytic formulas are hard.


26. Cross-Validation
Fun example first: instead of judging a singer from one performance, you judge across many stages.
In \(k\)-fold CV, split data into \(k\) parts, train on \(k-1\) parts, validate on the remaining part, repeat.
\[\text{CV Error} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \text{Error}_i\]
flowchart TD
    A[Dataset] --> B[Split into k folds]
    B --> C[Train on k-1 folds]
    B --> D[Validate on 1 fold]
    C --> E[Repeat k times]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Average score]
ML/AI use: better estimate of out-of-sample performance.


27. Bias-Variance Tradeoff
Fun example first: a model can be too simple (misses patterns) or too complex (memorizes noise).

High bias: underfitting.
High variance: overfitting.
Goal: balanced generalization.

Decomposition idea:
\[\text{Expected Error} \approx \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Noise}\]
ML/AI use: controls model complexity and regularization strategy.


28. Regularization (L1 and L2)
Fun example first: adding luggage fees forces you to pack only what matters.

L1 (Lasso) can shrink some coefficients to exactly zero.
L2 (Ridge) shrinks coefficients smoothly.

Formulas:
\[\text{Lasso: } \min \sum (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda\sum |\beta_j|\]
\[\text{Ridge: } \min \sum (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda\sum \beta_j^2\]
ML/AI use: combats overfitting and improves stability.


29. Entropy and Information Gain
Fun example first: a good yes/no question in a guessing game cuts uncertainty fast.
Entropy:
\[H(S) = -\sum_i p_i\log_2 p_i\]
Information gain:
\[IG = H(\text{parent}) - \sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}H(S_v)\]
ML/AI use: decision trees choose splits with high information gain.


30. PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
Fun example first: if you photograph a 3D object from the best angle, you still keep most shape information in 2D.
PCA finds directions (principal components) with maximum variance.
Optimization view:
\[\max_{\|w\|=1} \; w^T\Sigma w\]
ML/AI use: dimensionality reduction, visualization, denoising.


31. Outlier Detection with Z-Score and IQR
Fun example first: if one user clicks 10,000 times in a minute, that point deserves investigation.
Z-score:
\[z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\]
IQR rule:
\[x < Q1 - 1.5\cdot IQR \quad \text{or} \quad x > Q3 + 1.5\cdot IQR\]
ML/AI use: anomaly detection and robust data cleaning.


32. Which Method Should I Use First?
flowchart TD
    A[Start with your question] --> B{Target type?}
    B -->|Numeric| C[Regression / ANOVA / Correlation]
    B -->|Category| D[Chi-square / Logistic / Naive Bayes]
    B -->|No labels| E[Clustering / PCA]
    C --> F[Validate with CV and residual checks]
    D --> F
    E --> F






Tip



Quick reviewer rule: always ask three questions before trusting a result.

Is the data type correct for the test?
Are the assumptions reasonable?
Does the metric match the real-world cost of mistakes?

title: Statistics - Fundamentals
text:
Final Takeaway
Statistics is not just formulas. It is the discipline of asking better questions, measuring uncertainty honestly, and choosing the right tool for the data you actually have.
If you remember only one idea, remember this: describe first, infer carefully, and always check the assumptions before you trust the conclusion.
Bonus memory trick: if you are stuck, start with these four in order.

Plot the data.
Check spread and skew.
Pick a method that matches data type.
Validate with out-of-sample testing.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
Note



No Linux experience needed. Work with invented study records and tiny sequencing files. No patient data or paid software is needed for the core exercises. Examples target Bash on Ubuntu/Linux. Remote-server and specialist-tool examples are templates, clearly separated from runnable practice.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
1. Linux in plain language

Why
Before you analyze data, you must find the correct input, check it, run a program, and inspect its output. Linux makes these tasks repeatable on research servers, clinical platforms, and cloud computers.


What
An operating system manages files, memory, hardware, and programs. Linux is technically its core, the kernel. A distribution such as Ubuntu combines that kernel with useful software.








Word
Plain-language meaning
Example




Distribution
An installable Linux system
Ubuntu, Debian, Rocky Linux


Terminal
Window where you type commands
VS Code’s integrated terminal


Shell
Program that interprets your commands
Bash


Command
Instruction to a tool
pwd


Filesystem
Hierarchy of files and folders
/home/analyst/study


Server
Computer reached over a network
Institution’s analysis machine


HPC cluster
Computers managed by a scheduler
University Slurm cluster





How
Think of the terminal as a text-based file manager plus a programmable workbench. Instead of clicking a folder, type cd. Instead of opening a huge log, search it with grep.







Role
Daily Linux use




Bioinformatician
Check FASTQ inputs, run alignments, inspect pipeline logs


Clinical programmer
Organize inputs, launch approved R/SAS jobs, reconcile deliveries


Data scientist
Inspect datasets, manage environments, monitor model training



Linux supports reproducibility. It does not establish scientific validity or regulatory compliance by itself.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
2. Your learning to-do list

Why
Learning useful actions in order is easier than memorizing hundreds of commands.


What
Use this checklist as a learning route. You do not need to finish it in one sitting.


How

Open Bash and explain the operating system, terminal, and shell.
Read a command and find help.
Create the synthetic study in Section 6.
Navigate, copy, move, and delete safely.
Read, search, count, and compare files.
Combine commands and capture logs and exit statuses.
Check permissions, storage, memory, and processes.
Understand environments, remote access, and transfers.
Write and test a small script.
Recognize bioinformatics, clinical, and HPC workflow boundaries.
Complete the mini-project and explain its checks.

First session: Sections 1-10. Daily productivity: Sections 11-20. Applied practice: Sections 21-25. Section 25 is your quick reference.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
3. Open a safe Linux workspace

Why
You need a real Bash session before these commands will behave as described.


What
Choose one route. Windows PowerShell is not Bash. A macOS terminal is not automatically Linux, and some command options differ.


How







Your computer
Starting point




Windows
Ubuntu through WSL, following your organization’s installation policy


macOS
Approved Linux virtual machine or Linux development container


Linux
Open the Terminal application


Managed work computer
Ask for an approved training environment


GitHub Codespaces
Open Terminal > New Terminal; use synthetic data only



On a personally managed Windows machine, run this in administrator PowerShell, not Bash. Installation may require a restart and Ubuntu account setup:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
Inside Linux, inspect your environment:
uname -s
cat /etc/os-release
bash --version
whoami
uname -s should print Linux. cat displays the distribution information. bash --version identifies Bash; version numbers vary. whoami prints your account name. None changes your files.






Warning



Use approved systems for real study data. Never upload patient records, credentials, or proprietary research to public repositories or personal training services. De-identified data can still be sensitive.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
4. Read your first command

Why
Understanding command structure lets you adapt examples instead of copying blindly.


What
The usual structure is command options arguments. Options change behavior; arguments identify what to act on.


How
ls -lh /tmp
ls lists contents, -l requests details, -h makes sizes readable, and /tmp is the directory to inspect. Combined short options such as -lh mean the same as -l -h here.
A prompt might be analyst@server:~$. Do not type the prompt or its $. A prompt ending in # often indicates an administrator account; avoid one for practice.







Symbol or key
Meaning




~
Your home directory


. / ..
Current directory / parent directory


/
Filesystem root, and path separator


Ctrl+C
Interrupt the foreground command; not copy-to-clipboard here


Ctrl+D
End input; at an empty prompt it can close the shell


Up arrow
Recall a previous command


Tab
Complete a command or path when possible


#
Starts a shell comment when unquoted and in comment position



Names are case-sensitive: ADSL.csv and adsl.csv can be different files. Prefer names such as study_001. Quote paths containing spaces: ls "Study Files".

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
5. Find help and recover calmly

Why
You do not need to memorize every option; learn how to verify one.


What
Tools provide help; Bash has separate help for built-in commands.


How
ls --help
help cd
command -v bash
type cd
--help usually shows usage. help cd explains Bash’s built-in directory changer. command -v locates a tool, or returns failure if unavailable. type identifies a built-in, alias, or executable.
If available, man ls opens a manual. Search with /, type a term, press Enter, and quit with q. Minimal containers may not include manuals.







Symptom
First action




command not found
Check spelling, command -v, and the approved environment


No such file or directory
Check pwd, ls, spelling, and case


Permission denied
Inspect access; do not automatically add sudo


A > continuation prompt
A quote or command is incomplete; Ctrl+C cancels it


A viewer seems stuck
Try q if it is less or man


A running command seems stuck
Inspect before interrupting; partial output may remain

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
6. Create your synthetic practice study

Why
Tiny, predictable data lets you check whether each command worked.


What
Create four invented subject records, a tab-separated sample sheet, two toy sequencing reads, and a log. This is not patient data or a validated clinical data structure.


How
Run the whole block in Bash. It refuses to replace an existing practice study.
mkdir -p "$HOME/linux-life-sciences"
cd "$HOME/linux-life-sciences"
if [[ -e study_001 ]]; then
    printf 'study_001 already exists; keep it or choose a new practice folder.\n'
else
    mkdir -p study_001/{raw,scripts,results,logs,scratch}
    cd study_001
    cat > raw/subjects.csv <<'EOF'
subject_id,arm,age
S001,Placebo,34
S002,Drug,57
S003,Drug,46
S004,Placebo,62
EOF
    printf 'sample_id\tgroup\nS001\tcontrol\nS002\ttreated\n' > raw/samples.tsv
    cat > raw/reads.fastq <<'EOF'
@read001
ACGTACGT
+
IIIIIIII
@read002
GGCCTTAA
+
IIIIIIII
EOF
    printf 'INFO start\nWARNING low coverage\nERROR missing reference\nINFO end\n' > logs/demo.log
    printf 'Practice study created in %s\n' "$PWD"
fi
mkdir -p creates folders and missing parents. Bash expands {raw,scripts,results,logs,scratch} into five paths. cd changes location. $HOME is your home path; $PWD is your current directory. [[ -e ... ]] tests existence; if, else, and fi choose which commands run.
cat > file <<'EOF' writes the lines up to EOF into a file: a here-document. Quoting 'EOF' prevents variable substitution inside that data. printf writes formatted text: \n means newline, \t means tab. > creates or overwrites a file, which is why the existence guard matters.
Before later sections, return to the study root:
cd "$HOME/linux-life-sciences/study_001"
pwd
ls
Expected directories: logs, raw, results, scratch, and scripts.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
7. Navigate without getting lost

Why
Many analysis failures are commands run in the wrong directory.


What
An absolute path starts at /; a relative path starts from your current directory.


How
cd "$HOME/linux-life-sciences/study_001"
pwd
ls -lah
cd raw
ls
cd ..
pwd prints your location. ls -lah combines details, hidden names (-a), and readable sizes. cd raw enters the folder; cd .. returns to its parent.



Command
Everyday use




cd ~
Return home


cd -
Return to the previous directory


ls raw
Inspect without entering


ls -ld raw
Inspect the directory itself


realpath raw/subjects.csv
Resolve the absolute path on Linux



/home/analyst/study is an illustrative path, not one guaranteed to exist. The $HOME practice paths work with your actual account.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
section: 8. Create, copy, move, and delete safely
text:
8. Create, copy, move, and delete safely

Why
Keep received inputs unchanged and experiment on copies.


What
cp copies; mv moves or renames; rm removes. rm normally bypasses any recycle bin.


How
From the study root:
mkdir -p scratch/copy_demo
cp -i raw/subjects.csv scratch/copy_demo/subjects.csv
mv -i scratch/copy_demo/subjects.csv scratch/copy_demo/subjects_copy.csv
ls -l scratch/copy_demo
rm -i scratch/copy_demo/subjects_copy.csv
rmdir scratch/copy_demo
-i prompts before certain overwrites/removals; read and answer deliberately. rmdir removes only empty directories. cp -r source_directory destination_directory copies a tree, but inspect the destination first because an existing directory can change the resulting layout.
touch scratch/notes.txt creates an empty file if absent or updates timestamps if present. It is not an editor. Use VS Code or an approved editor to write text; nano scratch/notes.txt is another option if installed. In nano, save with Ctrl+O, confirm with Enter, and exit with Ctrl+X.






Warning



Before deleting, run pwd and list the exact target. Do not practice recursive force deletion or wildcard cleanup on study data. Removal is not an approved secure-erasure procedure.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
9. Read files without opening everything

Why
Do not load a multi-gigabyte dataset into a spreadsheet merely to inspect its beginning.


What
head previews the beginning; tail previews the end; less browses interactively. cat prints everything, so reserve it for small files.


How
head -n 3 raw/subjects.csv
tail -n 2 raw/subjects.csv
cat raw/samples.tsv
wc -l raw/subjects.csv
file raw/subjects.csv
The first preview shows the header, S001, and S002. The last shows S003 and S004. wc -l reports 5 newline characters: a header plus four records here. It is not a general CSV record counter because fields can contain newlines. file inspects file type, not scientific validity, and may be absent from minimal environments.
Try less raw/subjects.csv: search with /S003, advance with n, and quit with q. tail -f logs/demo.log follows a growing log; Ctrl+C stops following, not the separate analysis that writes it.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
section: 10. Find files and search their contents
text:
10. Find files and search their contents

Why
Finding a filename and finding a message inside a file are different tasks.


What
find searches paths. grep searches text lines.


How
find raw -type f -name '*.csv'
find raw -type f -name '*.fastq'
grep -n 'S002' raw/subjects.csv
grep -nE 'WARNING|ERROR' logs/demo.log
grep -nF 'S002,Drug' raw/subjects.csv
-type f matches regular files. Quote '*.csv' so find, not Bash, expands the pattern. Expect raw/subjects.csv and raw/reads.fastq in the first two searches.
grep -n includes line numbers: S002 is on line 3. -E enables extended regular expressions, where | means either alternative: log lines 2 and 3 match. -F treats a pattern literally. grep -rni --include='*.log' 'error' logs searches logs recursively (-r) without case sensitivity (-i). A matching message is evidence to inspect, not proof of run failure.
Do not count arbitrary FASTQ reads with grep '^@': quality lines can also begin with @. Use a FASTQ-aware tool, as explained in Section 21.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
11. Combine commands and capture output

Why
Small tools become powerful when combined, and saved output makes review easier.


What
Programs write normal output to stdout, diagnostic output to stderr, and return an exit status. Zero normally means success; interpret nonzero values using the tool’s documentation.


How
grep -nE 'WARNING|ERROR' logs/demo.log > results/flagged_messages.txt
cat results/flagged_messages.txt
printf 'Reviewed synthetic log\n' >> logs/review.log
cut -d, -f2 raw/subjects.csv | tail -n +2 | LC_ALL=C sort | uniq -c
The final pipeline prints two Drug and two Placebo records. cut -d, -f2 selects field two using comma separation; tail -n +2 skips the header; sort puts equal values together; uniq -c counts adjacent repetitions. LC_ALL=C gives this sort a stable byte-based ordering. This works for our simple CSV, not arbitrary quoted CSV.







Operator/tool
Meaning




|
Send stdout into the next command’s input


> / >>
Replace a file / append to it


2>
Redirect stderr


> logs/run.log 2>&1
Put stdout and stderr in one log; order matters


tee results/copy.txt
Copy input to both stdout and a file; overwrites the file unless -a is used


&&
Run the next command only after success


||
Run the next command only after failure


;
Run the next command regardless of status



if grep -q 'ERROR' logs/demo.log; then
    printf 'An ERROR message was found; review the log.\n'
else
    status=$?
    printf 'grep exit status: %s\n' "$status"
fi
-q suppresses output. grep returns 0 for a match, 1 for no match, and typically 2 for an error. $? holds the immediately previous command’s status; another command replaces it. The example prints the review message because the toy log contains ERROR.
Never write a command’s output back to its input with sort input.tsv > input.tsv: the shell can empty the file before sort reads it.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
12. Inspect tabular text carefully

Why
Sample sheets and simple summaries can be inspected quickly without launching an analysis application.


What
cut selects fields, awk filters and calculates, and sort plus uniq summarizes text. These do not implement all CSV quoting rules.


How
cut -f1 raw/samples.tsv
awk -F '\t' 'NR > 1 && $2 == "treated" { print $1 }' raw/samples.tsv
awk -F, 'NR > 1 { total += $3; count++ } END { if (count) print total / count }' raw/subjects.csv
Expected: the sample ID column including its header, then S002, then mean age 49.75. cut defaults to tabs. In awk, -F chooses the separator, NR is the record number, $1 is field one, and END runs after all records. $2 inside the single-quoted awk program is an awk field, not a Bash argument.
A real CSV record such as S001,"Placebo, blinded",34 breaks naive comma splitting. Use an approved CSV-aware library. Optional example requiring Python 3:
python3 - <<'PY'
import csv

with open("raw/subjects.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as input_file:
        subjects = list(csv.DictReader(input_file))
ages = [int(subject["age"]) for subject in subjects]
print(f"Subjects: {len(subjects)}; mean age: {sum(ages) / len(ages):.2f}")
PY
Expected: Subjects: 4; mean age: 49.75. Production readers also need rules for missingness, types, duplicate IDs, and allowed values.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
13. Compare files and verify integrity

Why
A familiar filename does not prove that a delivery contains the same bytes.


What
diff shows text differences, cmp compares bytes, and sha256sum makes and verifies checksums.


How
cp raw/subjects.csv scratch/subjects_check.csv
diff -u raw/subjects.csv scratch/subjects_check.csv
cmp raw/subjects.csv scratch/subjects_check.csv
sha256sum raw/subjects.csv > results/subjects.sha256
sha256sum -c results/subjects.sha256
The comparisons are silent on identical files and return zero. diff returns 1 for differences and a greater value for trouble. Checksum verification should print raw/subjects.csv: OK. Run from the study root because the manifest contains a relative path.
Checksums detect byte changes, including line endings. They do not prove authenticity if someone can replace both the file and manifest: receive expected checksums through a trusted channel. Byte-identical data can still be scientifically incorrect.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
14. Compress and package files

Why
Sequencing inputs and study deliveries are often compressed to reduce storage and transfer time.


What
gzip compresses, zcat reads gzip content, and tar packages a directory tree.


How
gzip -c raw/reads.fastq > scratch/reads.fastq.gz
gzip -t scratch/reads.fastq.gz
zcat scratch/reads.fastq.gz | head -n 8
tar -czf scratch/study_inputs.tar.gz raw
tar -tzf scratch/study_inputs.tar.gz
mkdir -p scratch/unpacked
tar -xzf scratch/study_inputs.tar.gz -C scratch/unpacked
gzip -c preserves the original and writes compressed bytes to stdout. Plain gzip file normally replaces the original with file.gz. gzip -t tests integrity and is normally silent on success.
For tar, -c creates, -t lists, -x extracts, -z uses gzip, -f introduces the archive filename, and -C chooses the extraction directory.
Compression is not encryption. Inspect an archive’s origin and paths before extraction; use an empty destination and never extract untrusted archives as administrator. For large streams, head can close the pipe early; upstream tools may report a broken pipe under pipefail even when a preview appears.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
15. Understand permissions before changing them

Why
Authorized collaborators need access; unrelated server accounts should not automatically receive it.


What
Traditional permissions apply to owner, group, and others. r, w, x mean read, write, execute. On directories, x means permission to traverse.


How
id
ls -ld raw
ls -l raw/subjects.csv
cp raw/subjects.csv scratch/private_subjects.csv
chmod 600 scratch/private_subjects.csv
ls -l scratch/private_subjects.csv
umask
id shows user/group identities. chmod 600 gives the owner read/write and removes traditional group/other permission bits. The practice copy’s listing should start -rw-------.







Mode/command
Typical meaning




600
Private file: owner read/write


640
Owner read/write, group read


700
Private directory: owner can list, modify, traverse


750
Owner full access, group list/traverse


chmod u+x scripts/count_subjects.sh
Add executable permission for the owner



umask displays the mask for newly created files. In a personal practice shell, umask 077 requests private creation defaults; it does not change existing files. Follow institutional defaults for shared projects.
ACLs, parent directories, shared mounts, and administrator privileges also affect access. Permissions are not encryption or an audit trail. Avoid chmod 777; do not change ownership or use sudo without an approved reason.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
16. Check storage, memory, and processes

Why
Correct code can fail because a filesystem is full or a job exceeds its memory allowance.


What
Inspect filesystem capacity, folder usage, memory, and your own processes separately.


How
df -h .
du -sh raw results scratch
free -h
ps -u "$USER" -o pid,etime,%cpu,%mem,args



Command
Question answered




df -h .
Free space on this filesystem?


du -sh raw results scratch
Disk usage of these directories?


free -h
Memory reported by this Linux environment?


ps ...
Processes belonging to this account?


top
Interactive activity view; quit with q


quota -s
Personal quota, if installed and supported here?



In ps, PID is a process ID, etime is elapsed time, and args shows the command. Container/cluster limits can be lower than the reported host capacity. Avoid repeatedly scanning huge shared trees with du.
To stop a process, identify its PID, owner, and purpose first. kill -TERM PID requests graceful termination after you replace PID with its numeric value. Do not paste the placeholder. Avoid starting with kill -9, which prevents cleanup. Cancel scheduled work through its scheduler instead.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
17. Manage software environments

Why
Different projects may need incompatible tool versions. One uncontrolled shared environment makes results difficult to reproduce.


What
System packages, Python environments, research package managers, and HPC modules solve different problems.


How
command -v python3
command -v Rscript
command -v samtools
printf '%s\n' "$PATH"
PATH lists directories searched for executables. A missing tool may need installation or activation of the correct environment.







Situation
Appropriate approach




Personally managed Ubuntu
Approved apt packages; these change the OS and may require admin rights


Python project
venv isolates Python packages, not the whole operating system


Bioinformatics project
Approved Conda/Mamba environment or container with recorded versions


HPC
Site-provided module system; names and versions are local


Validated clinical platform
Approved change control, not ad hoc upgrades



Optional exercise, if Python and its venv support are installed:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python --version
python -m pip --version
deactivate
source runs activation in the current shell. deactivate restores the previous environment. If support is missing, use the approved installation process. Never pipe an unknown downloaded installation script directly into Bash or upgrade production tools to satisfy a tutorial.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
18. Connect and transfer securely

Why
Run large analyses near the data on approved infrastructure rather than moving restricted inputs onto personal devices.


What
ssh opens a remote shell, scp copies files over SSH, and rsync synchronizes trees. They require installed tools, authorized accounts, and network access.


How
Templates only: replace the account, reserved example hostname, and paths with administrator-provided values. Run transfers from the local terminal unless you intend otherwise.
ssh analyst@analysis.example.org
Verify a new server’s host-key fingerprint through a trusted administrator before accepting it. After login, use hostname, whoami, and pwd to confirm your location. exit closes the remote shell.
scp raw/samples.tsv analyst@analysis.example.org:/approved/project/incoming/
rsync -av --dry-run results/ analyst@analysis.example.org:/approved/project/results/
rsync -av results/ analyst@analysis.example.org:/approved/project/results/
-a requests archive behavior, -v shows activity, and --dry-run previews without transferring. results/ means the directory’s contents; omitting its trailing slash can change the destination layout. Inspect the preview first. Do not casually add --delete, which can remove destination files.
Follow approved SSH-key/MFA practices. Never store passwords or private keys in Git or scripts. SSH protects transport, not destination authorization or retention; verify important transfers with trusted checksums.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
19. Run programs and retain logs

Why
Reproducibility needs the command, software version, inputs, outputs, and completion status, not just a screenshot.


What
Foreground, background, persistent-terminal, and scheduler jobs have different lifecycles.


How
These are templates requiring your own analysis scripts and approved installations:
Rscript scripts/analysis.R > logs/analysis.log 2>&1
python3 scripts/analysis.py > logs/python_analysis.log 2>&1
Run the relevant command, then immediately use printf 'Exit status: %s\n' "$?". Review logs and expected outputs too. These example scripts are not created by the practice exercise.
For a personal, non-HPC Bash session, the background pattern is:
python3 scripts/analysis.py > logs/background.log 2>&1 &
job_pid=$!
printf 'Started PID %s\n' "$job_pid"
wait "$job_pid"
job_status=$?
printf 'Job exit status: %s\n' "$job_status"
& starts the job; $! captures its PID; wait returns its completion status. jobs -l lists jobs in this shell. Backgrounding does not guarantee survival after logout.
Where installed and permitted, tmux new -s study opens a persistent session. Detach with Ctrl+B then D; return with tmux attach -t study. tmux does not allocate compute resources. For clusters, use Section 23; do not run heavy analyses on login nodes.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
section: 20. Write and test a defensive Bash script
text:
20. Write and test a defensive Bash script

Why
A small script makes repeated checks consistent and reviewable.


What
Count physical data lines in the known simple synthetic CSV. Refuse accidental overwrites. This is not a general clinical CSV validator.


How
From the practice root, create and run the script:
cat > scripts/count_subjects.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -ne 2 ]]; then
    printf 'Usage: bash count_subjects.sh INPUT.csv OUTPUT.txt\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi

input_path=$1
output_path=$2
if [[ ! -f "$input_path" || ! -r "$input_path" || ! -s "$input_path" ]]; then
    printf 'Input must be a readable, nonempty regular file: %s\n' "$input_path" >&2
    exit 1
fi
if [[ -e "$output_path" ]]; then
    printf 'Output already exists: %s\n' "$output_path" >&2
    exit 1
fi

subject_count=$(awk 'END { print NR - 1 }' "$input_path")
printf 'subject_count\n%s\n' "$subject_count" > "$output_path"
printf 'Wrote %s\n' "$output_path"
EOF
bash -n scripts/count_subjects.sh
bash scripts/count_subjects.sh raw/subjects.csv results/subject_count.txt
cat results/subject_count.txt
Expected:
subject_count
4







Element
Meaning




#!/usr/bin/env bash
Select Bash when executing the script directly


set -e
Exit on many unhandled failures; exceptions exist in conditionals and other contexts


set -u
Treat unset variable expansion as an error


set -o pipefail
Pipeline status reflects its rightmost failure, not just its last command


$#, $1, $2
Argument count, first argument, second argument


-f, -r, -s
Regular file, readable, nonempty tests


>&2
Send the message to stderr


exit 1 / exit 2
Explicit failure statuses chosen by this script


$(...)
Capture a command’s stdout


bash -n
Check syntax without execution



Negative tests: rerun with the same output path; expect status 1 and unchanged output. Supply a nonexistent input and a fresh output path; expect 1 and no output. Omit arguments; expect 2.
Strict mode is a guardrail, not correctness: grep with no match can intentionally return nonzero. The existence check protects ordinary reruns, not simultaneous writers racing for a path. Production output handling needs stronger controls.
For direct execution, use chmod u+x scripts/count_subjects.sh and then ./scripts/count_subjects.sh INPUT.csv OUTPUT.txt with actual paths and a fresh output. ./ explicitly identifies a file in the current directory.
To repeat a check across several files, use a loop instead of retyping commands:
for input_path in raw/subjects.csv raw/samples.tsv; do
    printf 'Checking %s\n' "$input_path"
    wc -l "$input_path"
done
for assigns each listed path to input_path; do and done surround the repeated commands. Expect 5 lines for subjects and 3 for the sample sheet. Keep "$input_path" quoted so a filename containing spaces remains one argument. Use loops for controlled file operations, not as a substitute for a workflow engine’s scheduling and recovery.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
21. Bioinformatics: inspect before computing

Why
Checking input types and integrity before an expensive alignment can save hours of cluster time.


What








Format
Usually contains
Suitable approach




FASTQ / FASTQ.gz
Read IDs, sequences, base qualities
FASTQ-aware statistics and QC


FASTA
Reference sequences
Sequence-aware checks and reference provenance


SAM / BAM / CRAM
Read alignments
samtools; reference access where required


VCF / BCF
Variant records and metadata
bcftools or another format-aware reader


BED / GTF / GFF
Intervals or annotations
Validate format and coordinate conventions





How
Start with the toy input:
head -n 8 raw/reads.fastq
awk 'END { print NR / 4 }' raw/reads.fastq
The answer is 2. Dividing lines by four works here because this file is known to contain complete, four-line records. It does not validate real FASTQ, reliably handle wrapped records, or establish paired-end consistency.
The following are real-work templates, requiring installed SeqKit, FastQC, samtools, or bcftools and your own files:
seqkit stats reads_R1.fastq.gz reads_R2.fastq.gz
fastqc --threads 2 --outdir results reads_R1.fastq.gz reads_R2.fastq.gz
samtools quickcheck -v aligned.bam
samtools flagstat aligned.bam
bcftools stats variants.vcf.gz > results/variants_stats.txt







Command
Purpose and limits




seqkit stats
Sequence counts/lengths; equal mate counts do not prove paired IDs agree


fastqc
QC reports; --threads 2 sets concurrency but does not allocate cluster CPUs


samtools quickcheck -v
Limited structural checks with problem reporting; does not read every alignment


samtools flagstat
Alignment-flag summaries; mapping rates need protocol-specific interpretation


bcftools stats
Variant summaries, not proof of biological validity



Preserve sample metadata, reference assembly/checksum, annotation version, tool versions, parameters, resource requests, and logs. Do not use cat or a text editor to interpret binary BAM or BCF data as plain text.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
section: 22. Clinical programming: traceable inputs and outputs
text:
22. Clinical programming: traceable inputs and outputs

Why
Clinical deliverables need traceability to approved inputs and specifications. Shell tools support this; they do not replace independent QC, SOPs, or validation.


What
Separate received inputs, programs, derived datasets, reports, logs, and review evidence. SDTM and ADaM are clinical data standards; XPT and SAS datasets need appropriate readers, not comma splitting.


How
Create an illustrative output structure and input manifest using synthetic files:
mkdir -p results/clinical_demo/{sdtm,adam,tlf,qc}
sha256sum raw/subjects.csv raw/samples.tsv > results/clinical_demo/input_manifest.sha256
sha256sum -c results/clinical_demo/input_manifest.sha256
date -u +'%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ'
tlf means tables, listings, and figures; qc means quality control. The manifest should verify both inputs as OK. date -u prints UTC; the format produces a timestamp such as 2026-10-18T09:30:00Z. A timestamp alone is not a trustworthy audit trail.
An actual R batch run might use this template, after the script and controlled environment exist:
Rscript --vanilla scripts/create_adsl.R > logs/create_adsl.log 2>&1
--vanilla suppresses normal startup customizations, including user profiles and saved workspace restoration. It does not pin package versions or validate analysis. Follow controlled-platform startup requirements rather than assuming this flag is always appropriate.
For SAS, the launcher, license, batch options, exit-status behavior, and log conventions are platform-specific. Use the approved launcher. Review errors, relevant warnings, and unexpected notes according to study rules.







Review question
Evidence needed beyond a successful command




Correct inputs?
Approved snapshot, manifest, transfer documentation


Controlled environment?
Approved R/SAS versions, package inventory, configuration


Completed processing?
Exit status, reviewed log, expected nonempty outputs


Correct results?
Specification checks, reconciliation, independent programming/QC


Reconstructable run?
Program version, parameters, provenance, controlled run record



Keep participant identifiers out of filenames, shell history, unnecessary logs, and public examples. Never edit received data merely to make a check pass. This guide is educational, not a validated GxP process or submission standard.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
23. HPC: use the scheduler

Why
Shared clusters need fair resource allocation. Login nodes support light interaction, not large alignments or model fits.


What
A scheduler starts work on compute nodes using requested CPUs, memory, and time. Slurm is common; PBS and LSF use other commands.


How
This is the content of a Slurm job file, for example scripts/qc.slurm, not commands to paste individually. It requires your own scripts/qc.py, an approved Python environment, and site-appropriate resources:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=study_qc
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err

set -euo pipefail
python3 scripts/qc.py
#SBATCH lines are directives read by sbatch, not Bash options. They must precede executable commands. %x becomes the job name and %j the job ID. Requesting two CPUs does not automatically make Python use two CPUs. Add site-required account, partition, environment setup, and application-specific thread options.
On a Slurm cluster, after creating the file, submit from the project directory:
mkdir -p logs
sbatch scripts/qc.slurm
squeue -u "$USER"
sbatch returns a submission ID, not proof of analysis success. squeue lists active jobs. scancel JOB_ID cancels after you replace JOB_ID with the actual ID. Where accounting exists, sacct -j JOB_ID --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS helps inspect completed work. The logs directory must exist before Slurm opens its output files.
Use resource values justified by your program and input size, then inspect actual usage before scaling up. Do not request every CPU by habit.

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
24. Mini-project: a reviewable study snapshot

Why
One short workflow connects navigation, calculations, logs, checksums, and verification.


What
Create a fresh output directory, record input checksums, summarize four synthetic subjects, and check the known answers without changing raw inputs. Requirements: Bash, standard Ubuntu tools, and Section 6 data. No R, Python, or scientific packages are needed.


How
Run the entire block. Parentheses create a subshell so directory changes and shell options stay local. mktemp -d creates a unique directory for each run.
(
    set -euo pipefail
    cd "$HOME/linux-life-sciences/study_001"
    run_dir=$(mktemp -d results/review_XXXXXX)

    sha256sum raw/subjects.csv raw/samples.tsv raw/reads.fastq > "$run_dir/inputs.sha256"
    date -u +'%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ' > "$run_dir/started_utc.txt"
    bash --version > "$run_dir/bash_version.txt"
    awk --version > "$run_dir/awk_version.txt" 2>&1 || awk -W version > "$run_dir/awk_version.txt" 2>&1

    awk -F, '
        NR > 1 { subjects++; total_age += $3; arms[$2]++ }
        END {
            print "metric,value"
            print "subjects," subjects
            printf "mean_age,%.2f\n", total_age / subjects
            print "Drug," arms["Drug"]
            print "Placebo," arms["Placebo"]
        }
    ' raw/subjects.csv > "$run_dir/summary.csv"

    grep -qxF 'subjects,4' "$run_dir/summary.csv"
    grep -qxF 'mean_age,49.75' "$run_dir/summary.csv"
    grep -qxF 'Drug,2' "$run_dir/summary.csv"
    grep -qxF 'Placebo,2' "$run_dir/summary.csv"
    sha256sum -c "$run_dir/inputs.sha256" > "$run_dir/integrity.log"
    printf 'PASS: expected synthetic summary and unchanged inputs\n' > "$run_dir/review.log"
    cat "$run_dir/summary.csv"
    cat "$run_dir/integrity.log"
    cat "$run_dir/review.log"
    printf 'Review files: %s\n' "$run_dir"
)
Expected summary:
metric,value
subjects,4
mean_age,49.75
Drug,2
Placebo,2
Expect three OK integrity checks and a review message starting PASS. grep -q is silent, -x requires a full-line match, and -F treats the expected text literally, including the decimal point. || runs the fallback awk version command only if the first fails: Ubuntu can provide GNU awk or mawk, which expose versions differently.
These checks assert known toy answers. If they fail, inspect the error and inputs; do not simply change expected values to obtain PASS. This example is not designed for empty, malformed, quoted, or real clinical CSV files.
Self-check: Why keep inputs separate? Why create a fresh run directory? Why do matching counts not prove correct data? Why is byte integrity different from statistical QC?

title: Linux — Foundations for Life Sciences Computing
text:
25. Daily reference and next steps

Why
Good notes should help when a job has failed and a deadline is close.


What
Use this reference after reading the relevant section. Paths refer to the synthetic study unless marked as templates.


How: daily command reference








Need
Command
Remember




Locate yourself
pwd
Check before modifying anything


Identify machine/account
hostname and whoami
Especially after remote login


List files
ls -lah
Includes hidden names


Enter the study
cd "$HOME/linux-life-sciences/study_001"
Quote paths


Create folders
mkdir -p results/qc
Cannot bypass protected parents


Copy a file
cp -i raw/subjects.csv scratch/subjects.csv
Preserve original inputs


Rename a copy
mv -i scratch/subjects.csv scratch/subjects_old.csv
Check overwrite prompts


Remove one file
rm -i scratch/subjects_old.csv
No ordinary undo


Remove empty folder
rmdir scratch/empty_folder
Fails if nonempty


Preview
head -n 5 raw/subjects.csv
Not validation


Inspect log end
tail -n 20 logs/demo.log
Follow with -f, stop with Ctrl+C


Browse text
less logs/demo.log
/ searches, q quits


Count newlines
wc -l raw/subjects.csv
Headers and multiline fields matter


Find files
find raw -type f -name '*.csv'
Quote the pattern


Search literally
grep -nF 'S002' raw/subjects.csv
-F means literal text


Extract TSV field
cut -f1 raw/samples.tsv
Not a CSV parser


Summarize simple text
awk -F, 'NR > 1 { print $2 }' raw/subjects.csv
Toy comma-separated text only


Count categories
cut -f2 raw/samples.tsv \| tail -n +2 \| sort \| uniq -c
Sort before uniq


Compare text
diff -u raw/subjects.csv scratch/subjects_check.csv
Exit 1 means different


Check bytes
sha256sum -c results/subjects.sha256
Correct working directory matters


Test gzip
gzip -t scratch/reads.fastq.gz
Silent success is normal


Inspect archive
tar -tzf scratch/study_inputs.tar.gz
Inspect before extracting


Check identities/access
id and ls -l raw/subjects.csv
Administrator rights are not the default fix


Private copy permissions
chmod 600 scratch/private_subjects.csv
Not encryption


Check free space
df -h .
Not your personal quota


Check folder usage
du -sh results
Avoid repeated scans of huge shared trees


Check memory
free -h
Check platform limits separately


Inspect own processes
ps -u "$USER" -o pid,etime,args
Confirm before stopping anything


Locate tool
command -v Rscript
Missing output means unresolved


Check script syntax
bash -n scripts/count_subjects.sh
Does not prove logic


Remote login, template
ssh analyst@analysis.example.org
Verify fingerprint; use real approved account


Transfer preview, template
rsync -av --dry-run results/ analyst@analysis.example.org:/approved/project/results/
Inspect before sending





How: troubleshoot in the right order








Symptom
Likely issue
Safe next step




File not found
Location, case, spelling
pwd, ls, inspect exact path


Command not found
Installation or environment
command -v, approved environment setup


Access denied
File, parent, ACL, execution restriction
id, ls -ld, ask owner


Disk full
Capacity or quota
df -h ., du -sh, quota check


Job killed or vanished
Memory/time limit, logout, administrator action
Logs and scheduler accounting


Wrong record count
Header, duplicates, delimiter, multiline fields
Preview and format-aware parsing


bad interpreter with ^M
Windows CRLF script line endings
Save script as LF in editor; leave raw inputs unchanged


No command output
Silent success or no matches
Check documented status and expected files


Checksum mismatch
Changed bytes or different delivery
Stop and reconcile; do not regenerate expected checksum to hide it


Partial output
Interrupted or failed analysis
Review status/logs; rerun to a fresh output location





How: a five-minute daily routine

Confirm machine, account, directory, and approved environment.
Confirm input identity, permissions, storage, and resource allocation.
Run the reviewed script with logs and explicit output locations.
Review completion status, logs, outputs, and scientific/domain QC.
Preserve provenance and deliver approved outputs through approved channels.

Read the GNU Bash manual, GNU Coreutils documentation, Ubuntu command-line introduction, and institutional HPC/data-handling guidance. Specialist references: samtools, SeqKit, and Slurm.
